page_hint: Ch 26 §8 (Mini-Case), Step 1 and Step 2; also §3 'Capstone Execution'
quoted_clause: The 450 ms is a *service-time sum with no queueing term*; at the offered ~2 rps against the ~2.0 req/s analytical ceiling (ρ near 1), a real queueing delay sits on top ... the baseline's 320 ms compute is a worst-case figure carrying prefill-queue inflation at ρ near 1, and the miss value assumes that queue has drained at the cached ~1.3 rps (compute falls from the inflated 320 ms to ~120 ms, so 250 ≈ 120 + 80 + 50) ... (both sides are service-time sums with no queueing term — at ρ near 1 a real queue would sit on top of the baseline too)
observed: The baseline's 450 ms is asserted to contain no queueing term, while its 320 ms compute component is asserted to carry prefill-queue inflation at ρ near 1. Both statements cannot hold. The cached/miss side (250 ms) is explicitly queue-drained, so the headline comparison is a queue-inflated baseline against a queue-drained treatment — and the chapter twice claims both sides are queue-free.
evidence: Step 1: 320 + 80 + 50 = 450 ms, declared 'a service-time sum with no queueing term'. Step 2: the 320 ms term is 'a worst-case figure carrying prefill-queue inflation at ρ near 1', and the miss value 'assumes that queue has drained at the cached ~1.3 rps'. Step 2 then asserts 'both sides are service-time sums with no queueing term'. §3 repeats the same claim. The offered load in Step 1 is ~2 rps against a ~2.0 req/s ceiling (ρ ≈ 1), the regime the chapter itself says produces unbounded queueing delay.
root_cause: The baseline was authored as a queue-free service-time sum, then re-described as queue-inflated when the miss path needed a smaller compute term. The two framings were never reconciled, and the reconciliation was then asserted away in prose.
correction: Choose one baseline definition and state it once. Either (a) baseline = queue-free service-time sum of 450 ms (320 ms compute with no queue inflation), in which case the miss path must be re-derived on the same queue-free basis and the 120 ms compute figure justified independently; or (b) baseline = queue-inflated, in which case the cached side must also be evaluated at ρ ≈ 1, or the comparison must be explicitly labelled 'queue-drained treatment vs queue-inflated baseline'. Then restate the −44% on the reconciled basis.
acceptance_test: One sentence in Step 1 defines the baseline's queue treatment; Step 2's 250 ms and the −44% use the same treatment; a reader can recompute both sides from the printed components and reproduce the same percentage.

quoted_clause: compute falls from the inflated 320 ms to ~120 ms, so 250 ≈ 120 + 80 + 50
observed: The mechanism by which per-request compute drops from 320 ms to 120 ms when offered load falls from ~2.0 rps to ~1.3 rps is asserted but not explained. The reader is not told whether the drop comes from reduced resource contention, reduced queue-wait time, smaller effective batch size, or some combination.
evidence: The text states the drop (320→120 ms) and attributes it to 'the queue has drained at the cached ~1.3 rps' but never specifies the physical mechanism. At ρ = 0.65 (1.3/2.0), queuing theory predicts shorter queues, but the text has already stated the 450 ms baseline has 'no queueing term,' so the reader cannot reconcile the two.
root_cause: The causal link between load reduction and compute-time reduction is left implicit.
correction: Add one sentence explaining the mechanism, e.g. 'At ρ near 1 the GPU time-slices prefill work across many concurrent requests, inflating each request's wall-clock prefill time; at 1.3 rps the contention eases and prefill returns to its uncontended ~120 ms.' Ensure this is consistent with the 'no queueing term' framing from CH26-03.
acceptance_test: The reader can explain why compute time decreases when load decreases, and the explanation is consistent with the 'no queueing term' statement.

quoted_clause: *Deeper continuous batching on the single host instead of sharding* raises throughput by lengthening the in-flight queue, adding queueing delay exactly where the p99 TTFT SLO binds
observed: Two errors. (i) Continuous batching raises throughput by keeping the decode batch occupied (admitting a new request as another completes), not by 'lengthening the in-flight queue'; a longer queue is a symptom of saturation, not the mechanism of higher throughput. (ii) On this host the resident-request ceiling is set by KV residency (C ≈ 17.5 within the ~436 GB KV budget of the ~500 GB non-weight pool), so 'deeper' batching cannot add resident requests at all — it can only add queueing delay and prefill interference. The alternative is infeasible on this host, not merely harmful.
evidence: §3 Pattern A: 'can hold ~17.5 concurrent 9,500-token requests within the canonical ~436 GB KV budget from Chapter 15'; 640 GB pool − 140 GB weights = 500 GB, of which ~436 GB is KV. §3 Alternatives: the deeper-batching rejection as quoted.
root_cause: The rejection reason was written as a generic queueing argument without checking the host's binding constraint, which the same chapter establishes two paragraphs earlier.
correction: Rewrite the rejection around the binding constraint: 'the host's resident-request capacity is already KV-bound at C ≈ 17.5 (Ch 15); deeper batching cannot raise concurrency, only queueing delay and prefill interference, so it cannot raise throughput on this host.' If the intent is to compare against a host with more KV headroom, say so and quantify the headroom required.
acceptance_test: The rejection names the binding constraint (KV residency) and does not attribute throughput gain to queue length; a reader can confirm from C ≈ 17.5 that concurrency is capped.

acceptance_test: The reader can determine which parameter count is claimed to be unchanged and verify it against stated figures.

quoted_clause: | Inference Sharding | SM utilization % | per-GPU token latency p99 | All-Reduce time | | Semantic Response Cache | hit ratio @ TTL=T | stale read rate | cache memory pressure | | Circuit Breaker | timeout count / 30s | fallback activation rate | recovery grace-period latency |
